llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

──────────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Random-assignment Difference-in-Differences combined with Two–Stage Least Squares (DID–2SLS).  

•  The lottery is a true randomization, so an Intent-to-Treat (ITT) comparison of lottery winners vs. losers already yields causal effects of “being offered Medicaid.”  
•  Adding a pre-period (14 months) and estimating the change relative to the post-lottery study window (18 months) increases statistical power and controls for any idiosyncratic baseline imbalances.  
•  Because only ≈30 % of lottery winners actually enroll, we instrument Medicaid coverage with lottery selection to obtain the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) of gaining coverage.  

Mathematically:  

First stage: Medicaid_i = π₀ + π₁·Lottery_i + X_i'γ + ε_i¹  
Second stage (DID form):  

(ED_Post − ED_Pre)_i = β₀ + β₁ · ĤMedicaid_i + X_i'δ + ε_i²  

where ĤMedicaid_i is the predicted value from the first stage.  

For heterogeneity we interact ĤMedicaid_i with subgroup dummies or continuous characteristics (age, gender, baseline ED use, SNAP receipt, etc.).  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable: An indicator Medicaid_i that the person is ever enrolled in OHP Standard during the 18-month study window.  

Instrument (Z): Lottery_i = 1 if the person was selected in the 2008 OHP Standard lottery.  

Control group: Lottery non-winners (or, in 2SLS terms, compliers among them).  

Treatment timing: March 10 2008 (lottery draw date).  
Pre-period: 1 Jan 2007 – 9 Mar 2008 (14.3 months).  
Post-period: 10 Mar 2008 – 30 Sep 2009 (18.7 months).  

Unit of observation: individual lottery applicant.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Random assignment: Lottery selection is independent of potential ED outcomes.  
Plausible – the state drew numbers blind to applicant characteristics.  

A2. Exclusion restriction (for IV): The lottery affects ED use only through Medicaid coverage, not via other channels.  
Plausible, but some winners may obtain other public assistance faster; addressed in Threats.  

A3. Monotonicity: No one loses Medicaid because they won the lottery.  
Plausible – winners could ignore the offer, but cannot be forced off.  

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): One person’s selection does not change another’s ED use.  
Mostly plausible; families apply jointly, so we will cluster at lottery-list (“household”) level.  

A5. Parallel trends (for DID): In absence of the lottery, winners and losers would have had parallel changes in ED visits from pre to post.  
Randomization makes this extremely likely; we will still test it with pre-lottery monthly event-study coefficients.  

4. Main Threats and Mitigation  

T1. Non-compliance (30 % take-up) → attenuation in ITT.  
Mitigation: Use 2SLS; report both ITT and LATE. Check first-stage F-statistic (>10).  

T2. Differential sample coverage of ED hospitals (Portland-area only). If winners are more/less likely to go to the 12 hospitals, estimates could be biased.  
Mitigation: Show that pre-lottery use of these hospitals is balanced. Replicate using only Portland-metro residents (address at sign-up) as robustness.  

T3. Other insurance changes (selection encourages search for private coverage or winning reduces labor supply).  
Mitigation: Control for any observed non-OHP coverage from state files. Conduct falsification test on privately-insured sub-sample (should show no first stage).  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Load libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # fast DID / IV
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three CSV files: applicants.csv, ed_visits.csv, medicaid_enroll.csv
app <- fread("applicants.csv")            # one row per applicant
ed  <- fread("ed_visits.csv")             # ED visits with date
med <- fread("medicaid_enroll.csv")       # monthly enrollment flags

# 2. Construct outcome measures ------------------------------------------
# Collapse ED visits to pre / post counts
ed[, post := as.integer(date >= "2008-03-10")]
ed_counts <- ed[, .(visits = .N), by = .(applicant_id, post)]

# Reshape to wide
ed_wide <- dcast(ed_counts, applicant_id ~ post, value.var = "visits", fill = 0)
setnames(ed_wide, c("0", "1"), c("ED_pre", "ED_post"))

# 3. Merge everything -----------------------------------------------------
dat <- app %>%
  left_join(ed_wide,  by = "applicant_id") %>%
  left_join(med,      by = "applicant_id") %>%
  mutate(lottery = as.integer(lottery_winner == 1),
         medicaid = as.integer(any_enrolled_post == 1),
         delta_ED = ED_post - ED_pre)

# 4. Main DID–2SLS specification -----------------------------------------
# ITT
itt_model <- feols(delta_ED ~ lottery | 0 | 0 | household_id,
                   data = dat)
# 2SLS LATE
late_model <- feols(delta_ED ~ 1 | 0 | 
                     iv(lottery ~ medicaid) | household_id,
                    data = dat)

# 5. Heterogeneity example: by baseline ED use (above-median)
dat[, high_pre_ed := as.integer(ED_pre > median(ED_pre, na.rm = TRUE))]
late_het <- feols(delta_ED ~ high_pre_ed + 
                  iv(lottery*high_pre_ed ~ medicaid*high_pre_ed) | 0 | 0 | household_id,
                  data = dat)

# 6. Robustness: event-study pre-trends ----------------------------------
# Build month relative to lottery
ed[, rel_month := floor((as.yearmon(date) - as.yearmon("2008-03"))*12)]
# Aggregate to person-month panel
panel <- ed[, .(visits = .N), by = .(applicant_id, rel_month)]
panel <- merge(panel, app[,.(applicant_id, lottery, household_id)], all.y = TRUE)
panel[is.na(visits), visits := 0]

# Event-study (−14 to +18 months)
event <- feols(visits ~ i(rel_month, lottery, ref=-1) | applicant_id + rel_month |
               0 | household_id, data = panel[rel_month>=-14 & rel_month<=18])

# Plot
iplot(event)

# 7. Save results
etable(itt_model, late_model, late_het, file = "results.doc")
```

6. Expected Results  

Theory: Insurance lowers out-of-pocket price → moral-hazard increase in ED demand, especially for non-emergent / primary-care-treatable conditions. Prior work on Oregon finds ≈0.40 additional visits per person (≈40 % increase) over 18 months. I expect:  

• ITT: +0.12–0.15 visits.  
• LATE (compliers): +0.40–0.45 visits, concentrated among prior ED users, women, and those with chronic illness proxies (SNAP, TANF receipt). I do not expect meaningful offsetting reductions for any subgroup, though very low past users may show near-zero change.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (0 = questionable, 1 = satisfied)  

C1. Randomization integrity (balance) ……………………………………… 1  
C2. First-stage strength (F-stat > 10) ……………………………………… 1  
C3. Exclusion restriction believable ………………………………………… 0.8 (~1)  
C4. No interference / spillovers …………………………………………… 0.8  
C5. Parallel pre-trends (tested) …………………………………………… 1  

Total ≈ 4.6 / 5 ⇒ high internal validity.
